extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American political history and political science
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive analysis of the composition, behavior, and durability of American political parties (major and minor) around the late 19th–early 20th century, explaining why parties form, persist, split, and how minor parties operate. Useful for understanding party dynamics and classification in U.S. politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a national party
rubrics_metrics.description: Any section of men who nominate candidates of their own for the presidency and vice-presidency of the United States are deemed a national party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a simple, explicit test for classifying a group as a 'national party.' Examples cited: Greenbackers, Prohibitionists, Labour/Socialist parties when they held national nominating conventions and put forward presidential tickets. Explains that groups not running a presidential ticket (e.g., Mugwumps) are not national parties by American use of the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical coextensiveness as characteristic of major parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The two great parties (Republicans and Democrats) are absolutely co-extensive with the Union: they exist in every State and corner, and even in the Territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This coextensiveness distinguishes major parties from minor ones and underpins their national reach and stability. The text contrasts this feature with minor parties which 'did not attempt to maintain organizations all over the Union.' It is given as a reason why the two-party system endures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational scope of minor parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor parties typically do not maintain organizations across the Union and are often strong only in limited regions or a subset of States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and statistics: in 1908 the Socialist party cast votes in every State except Vermont; Prohibitionists obtained votes in 39 States; Populists in 16. The guidance explains that limited geographic organization constrains a minor party's national influence but allows regional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor parties' practical strategies: run local/state tickets or fuse with major parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor parties may run candidates for State and city offices where strong, or they may 'fuse' temporarily with one of the regular parties to obtain practical results and office for their nominees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Populists and Democrats 'fused' in six states in 1892 to mutual advantage; minor parties often prefer fusion to independent runs to secure tangible offices. This is presented as a pragmatic survival or influence tactic rather than a sign of being a national party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor parties as vote-draws or safety-valves
rubrics_metrics.description: A minor party/ticket can draw away votes from a major party in a doubtful State, potentially deciding elections; alternatively, it can act as a safety-valve preventing 'bolters' from voting for the opposite party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases: Prohibitionist votes possibly harmed Blaine in 1884; Mugwumps' defection in 1884 shifted New York to Cleveland. The text explains both the spoiler effect and the safety-valve mitigating more dangerous defection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for the persistence and stability of the two-party system
rubrics_metrics.description: American parties are stable partly because they are not based on differences of wealth or social strata (their cleavage is vertical rather than horizontal), and because the existence of active opposing parties across regions prevents any single sectional victory from being felt as a defeat by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that geographic diversity and vertical cleavages reduce risks of political severance or class-based fragmentation. Compares with English politics (stability and good feeling between classes). Notes potential threat if a new socialist or labour party were to absorb an existing major party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why purely local or sectional parties fail nationally
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties founded on a single region, local interest, or particular trade interest are unlikely to become national parties because their localism is viewed as anti-national and would have little support across the vast Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the normative American hostility to sectionalism (recalling the disunionist spirit) and the practical electoral problem of being outvoted by national parties. However, such local factions can still wield influence by controlling votes in their region and extracting concessions from national parties (e.g., anti-Asiatic legislation promised to Pacific coast electorates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnic, religious, and demographic tendencies in party alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular ethnic, religious, and demographic groups tend to align with specific parties (e.g., Scandinavians and Germans often Republican; French Canadians and Roman Catholics often Democratic; Negroes largely Republican in gratitude for Civil War-era policies; Mormons vote under church direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives region- and group-specific illustrations: Scandinavians in Upper Mississippi States, French Canadians in New England, negroes' significance in certain Northern States and decline in the South after disfranchisement, Mormons in Utah/Idaho/Arizona. Also notes intra-group nuances (e.g., shifts due to People's Party, or religious influence producing occasional deviations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greenbackers' defining issue and support base
rubrics_metrics.description: Greenbackers demanded a large issue of greenbacks (paper money) believing more money in circulation would benefit poorer classes; their support came largely from small farmers and some workers after the Civil War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the economic rationale as perceived by supporters, notes historical context (depreciation during/after Civil War, who wins/loses from such policy), and recounts Greenbackers' national conventions (1876, 1880, 1884) and eventual melting away and absorption into other movements (Populists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour and Socialist parties' varied tenets and bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour/Socialist parties are composed chiefly of urban and mining working men (including many recent immigrants) with diverse views, advocating reforms such as nationalization of land, progressive income tax, public ownership of railroads/telegraphs, restriction of immigration under contract, limits on monopolies, currency expansion, and statutory restriction of hours of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that not all leaders or followers adopt all tenets; the party tends to split into factions; its strength lies in trade unions (Knights of Labour) and in immigrant urban communities. Presents electoral history: late entry into presidential politics, small but occasionally decisive vote totals in state/city contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitionists' aims and political role
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitionists oppose the sale of intoxicating liquors and have run national conventions for presidential nominations since 1872, but their main political action has been at the State level (liquor regulation being a State matter); they have also proposed a Federal constitutional amendment to ban liquor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes platform excerpt (1892) calling for entire suppression of manufacture, sale, importation, exportation, transportation of alcoholic liquors; explains their typical small presidential vote but frequent influence in state legislatures and moral/ religious base; distinguishes Prohibitionists proper from broader Temperance men and notes ties to women's suffrage advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Populists/People's Party agrarian program and trajectory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Farmers' Alliance/People's (Populist) Party arose from agrarian discontent, combining elements of Greenbacker and Labour demands, seeking reduced taxation on real estate and public loans to farmers at low interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records rapid rise in 1889–1890 with seats in Congress and a presidential candidacy in 1892 (carrying four States), followed by decline (29,108 votes in 1908). Notes tendency for agrarian outbreaks to reappear but also movement toward more collectivist-type parties in the era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mugwumps as a temporary tendency rather than a party
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mugwumps were a temporary secession/tendency in 1884 of Republicans who bolted their party (some abstained, some voted for Prohibitionist St. John, many for Democrat Cleveland) but did not form a national party because they did not run their own ticket or maintain permanent machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains their influence (possibly decisive in New York 1884), organizational pattern (committees that dissolved post-election), and their later absorption back into regular parties or into Democrats in parts of the North. Use as example of a 'tendency' that can be electorally important without becoming a national party.
